## Description

The Lin-Bairstow method finds the roots of a real polynomial $P(x) = a_n x^n + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0$ two at a time, by finding a quadratic factor $x^2 - rx - s$.
It uses only real arithmetic, yet finds complex-conjugate pairs of roots as well as real ones.

Dividing $P(x)$ by $x^2 - rx - s$ leaves a quotient $Q(x)$ and a remainder,

$$
P(x) = (x^2 - rx - s)\,Q(x) + b_1 (x - r) + b_0, \qquad Q(x) = b_n x^{n-2} + \cdots + b_3 x + b_2 ,
$$

where quadratic synthetic division computes the $b$'s, and the same recursion applied to the $b$'s gives the $c$'s:

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_n &= a_n, & b_{n-1} &= a_{n-1} + r\,b_n, & b_k &= a_k + r\,b_{k+1} + s\,b_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 1, 0), \\
c_n &= b_n, & c_{n-1} &= b_{n-1} + r\,c_n, & c_k &= b_k + r\,c_{k+1} + s\,c_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 2, 1).
\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic is a factor exactly when $b_0 = b_1 = 0$, and the method is Newton's method on these two equations in $r$ and $s$.
The $c$'s are the partial derivatives ($\partial b_0/\partial r = c_1$, $\partial b_0/\partial s = \partial b_1/\partial r = c_2$, $\partial b_1/\partial s = c_3$), so each step evaluates them at $(r_j, s_j)$ and solves, by Cramer's rule in Mathews' module,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} c_1 & c_2 \\ c_2 & c_3 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \Delta r \\ \Delta s \end{pmatrix}
= -\begin{pmatrix} b_0 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad r_{j+1} = r_j + \Delta r, \quad s_{j+1} = s_j + \Delta s .
$$

The method needs degree $n \ge 3$, a starting guess $(r_0, s_0)$, and $c_1 c_3 - c_2^2 \neq 0$ at every iterate.
Real starts keep the iterates real, and a real polynomial always has a real quadratic factor.
Mathews suggests $r_0 = -a_1/a_2$, $s_0 = -a_0/a_2$ (if $a_2 \neq 0$), from $P(x) \approx a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$ near $x = 0$.

In general, Newton's method for a smooth system converges quadratically from close enough starts when its Jacobian is nonsingular at the solution.
Here that holds exactly when $x^2 - rx - s$ and $Q(x)$ have no common root, as when every root of $P$ is simple.
When they share one, convergence can drop to linear: for $P(x) = (x^2 + 1)^2$ from $(0.1, -1.2)$, the error ratio tends to $1/2$.

For Mathews' Example 4, $P(x) = x^4 + x^3 + 3x^2 + 4x + 6$ from $(r_0, s_0) = (-2.1, -1.9)$, the iterates converge to $x^2 + 2x + 2$, with roots $-1 \pm i$, and $Q(x) = x^2 - x + 3$ gives $\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{11}}{2} i$.
From step 2 on, the error's exponent roughly doubles each step (errors from 40-digit arithmetic):

| $j$ | $r_j$ | $s_j$ | error $\lVert (r_j + 2,\, s_j + 2) \rVert$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | −2.1 | −1.9 | $1.41 \times 10^{-1}$ |
| 1 | −1.989302820836 | −1.949988192338 | $5.11 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| 2 | −1.999992769905 | −2.000150979221 | $1.51 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | −1.999999996545 | −1.999999991124 | $9.52 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| 4 | −2.000000000000 | −2.000000000000 | $1.42 \times 10^{-17}$ |

Repeating the method on $Q(x)$ (deflation) finds the rest.
For the quintic $x^5 + 6x^4 - 20x^2 + 22x + 8$ of Mathews' Examples 1–3, the start $(-2, 3)$, his divisor $x^2 + 2x - 3$, gives $x^2 + 3.238964x + 0.853460$ (roots $-2.949618$, $-0.289346$); his suggested start on the cubic quotient gives $x^2 - 2.301046x + 1.851731$ (roots $1.150523 \pm 0.726655i$), leaving $x + 5.062082$.

Convergence is only local.
From $(r_0, s_0) = (-1, -2)$ on the same quintic, the iterates are thrown out to $|s_{26}| \approx 7 \times 10^8$ and wander for more than 90 steps, and the factor they reach depends on the arithmetic: $x^2 - 2.301046x + 1.851731$ in double precision, $x^2 + 8.011701x + 14.931211$ with 30 or more digits.

Quadratic synthetic division extends the division by $x - c$ of [Horner's Method](../horners-method.qmd), the iteration is two-variable [Newton-Raphson](../newton-raphson-method/) as in [Nonlinear Systems](../nonlinear-systems/), [Graeffe's Method](../graeffes-method/) is another method made for polynomials, and [Muller's Method](../mullers-method/) can also reach complex roots, using complex arithmetic.
